title: The man who held the reins
told: a sakhi of Guru Nanak and Bhai Lehna, a traditional story

hook.say: before the story, a question. what’s the first thing you hear in the morning?
options: me too. this one might change that. listen.

steps.line: Before dawn in the village of Khadur, a man named Lehna heard his neighbor reciting a long poem. He stopped at the door, and couldn’t move.
steps.label: a traditional sakhi

steps.line: It was Japji Sahib, Guru Nanak’s morning prayer. Can you think your way to God? Not if you think a hundred thousand times, it says.

steps.q: Lehna was already devout. Every year he led pilgrims to the goddess. Why would this poem stop him?
o: It asked what his pilgrimages hadn’t answered
It promised a quicker road to God
It praised the goddess he served
steps.why: He had been searching for years, and the poem spoke to the search itself. The neighbor reciting it, Bhai Jodha, was a Sikh of Guru Nanak.

steps.line: On his next pilgrimage, he turned his horse toward Kartarpur, where Guru Nanak lived, to meet the poet himself.
Near the village he asked an old man the way. The old man took the horse’s reins and walked him all the way there.

steps.q: Lehna walks into the hall. On the Guru’s seat sits the old man from the road. What does Lehna do?
o: Begs pardon, then rides on to the goddess
Gives up his pilgrimage for good
steps.why: He never finished the trip. The Guru had walked the whole way so his guest could ride, and the pilgrims’ leader stayed to serve.

steps.line: Inside, he looked up at the Guru’s seat. It was the old man who had walked beside his horse.
Lehna was ashamed: he had ridden while the Guru walked. He never went on with his pilgrimage. Years later, he became the second Guru, Guru Angad.

steps.q: Guru Nanak gave Lehna a new name, Angad, and chose him over his own sons. What does Angad mean?
steps.why: Ang means limb. Guru Nanak named him part of his own body, and in 1539 Guru Angad became the second Guru.

steps.q: As the second Guru, Angad is remembered for something Sikhs use every day. What?
steps.why: Tradition credits Guru Angad with shaping Gurmukhi, the script the Guru Granth Sahib is written in. He and his wife, Mata Khivi, also kept the free kitchen, langar, running.

say: japji sahib opens the guru granth sahib. it starts with the root verse, then thirty-eight stanzas called pauris, steps, like a ladder.
many sikhs recite it every morning, often from memory, before the day begins. and nobody starts with all of it. you start with a line, then a stanza, then a little more.

steps.q: From the story, what did Guru Nanak teach Lehna before saying a single word?
o: A seeker must earn his welcome
Pilgrimage is a waste of time
steps.why: Before any lesson, he served his guest. The teaching was the walk.

today.say: today, or tomorrow at dawn, let the first words you hear be good ones. before your phone, try one line of a morning prayer, japji’s opening or any line sacred to you. listen, read or recite. your choice.
options: one line is a whole first step.
then let it be the first thing on your commute.

sources: Traditional sakhi of Bhai Lehna (later Guru Angad) hearing Bhai Jodha recite Guru Nanak’s bani in Khadur and riding to Kartarpur, his horse led by Guru Nanak
Japji Sahib, Guru Nanak, Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1-8; first pauri (sochai soch na hovaee je sochee lakh vaar) paraphrased, Ang 1
check: Tellings differ on what Bhai Jodha recited (often Japji, sometimes Asa di Var); please confirm.
Lehna’s yearly pilgrimage to the goddess (often said to be Jwalamukhi) is tradition; I left the shrine unnamed.
